speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources whether the Ministry is keeping a close monitoring on the development of the recent air pollution incident in Pasir Gudang and whether it will affect Singapore given the close proximity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources in light of the Pasir Gudang chemical spill in March 2019 (a) how does the air and water quality in Sengkang, Punggol, Pasir Ris and Pulau Ubin compare with other parts of Singapore from 2008 to 2018, particularly during the northeast monsoon seasons; and (b) what contingency plans are there in the event of an environmental disaster in Johor affecting residents in the aforesaid areas.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The National Environment Agency (NEA) monitors and reports the air quality in Singapore through a network of five national air quality monitoring stations across the island.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These stations are representative of the ambient air quality of the North, South, East, West and Central regions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Criteria pollutants, namely, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone and particulate matter (PM), both PM2.5 and PM10, are continuously monitored and reported on an hourly basis as the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition, NEA monitors the coastal water quality continuously through buoy-based monitoring sensors deployed in eight locations around Singapore, including the Straits of Johor.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is supplemented by monthly collection samples from 48 sampling points around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA and SCDF are in contact with Malaysia’s Department of Environment (DOE) and Fire and Rescue Department (BOMBA) on this latest incident and will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates if there are significant developments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our agencies have put in place precautionary measures to guard against any potential pollution impacts arising from chemical incidents, including those from transboundary sources.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA’s existing air monitoring stations in the northeast region are able to measure the ambient concentration of a variety of VOCs, including benzene, toluene and xylene, in the parts per billion range.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These capabilities, and with the support of SCDF’s portable detectors, should allow us to detect a transboundary plume and to alert our population accordingly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to media reports, the Johor Chief Minister Dr Sahruddin Jamal had announced yesterday that the state government is looking into relocating their high-risk chemical factories.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Both NEA and SCDF are aware of the kinds of chemical industries existing today in Pasir Gudang.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is our existing arrangement to inform each other to ensure that if there are movements of major complexes, we inform each other.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, in this case, when they do and if they do relocate, we will be informed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first question is pertaining to the answer to a Parliamentary Question that the Minister gave in April this year with regard to the deployment of chemical gas detectors in the northeast area.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are there any plans that NEA has to make this deployment permanent in view of repeated environmental concerns that are raised in Johor, in particular about incidents that happen affecting school children and members of the public there?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to whether the Ministry is conducting any studies on low, constant exposure to VOCs, given the large number of residential homes in the Sengkang, Punggol and Pasir Ris region, in particular, and the northeast in general.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry pursuing any studies in this regard?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry aware of how many of these are considered to be high risk by internationally accepted standards?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As I had said, all the monitoring stations that I mentioned just now are permanent deployments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are to detect the ambient levels of VOCs as well as the pollutants in our air.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, when there are complaints from residents of persistent odours or smell that inconvenience them or cause them alarm, SCDF would also then put in the monitoring instruments to ensure that these are either non-existent or, if they are detected, to take the appropriate measures to advise accordingly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As for low constant VOCs, there are very few studies available to advise how much of it should be of concern to us at the ambient level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, all countries except one that we know of, do not even publish their VOCs on their websites.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Actually, many of us are, in one form or another, already exposed to VOCs on a daily basis like from the glues and the things that we handle regularly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, when we publish, for example, the PSI, it is based on benchmarks that have been established from proper medical impact of such pollutants or chemicals by bodies like the World Health Organization (WHO) and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) from the US.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Can I ask the Member to repeat the last question?
